The Great Exchange
thuh grayt eks-CHAYNJ
doctrinal phrase
From great and exchange (a mutual giving and receiving); a settled term for the double imputation at the heart of the gospel.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Great Exchange is the church’s name for the wondrous transaction at the heart of justification, summed up in the apostle’s words: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” In this exchange two things pass at once. Our sin and guilt were laid upon Christ, who, though He knew no sin of His own, was made sin for us and bore in His body on the tree the curse and condemnation we deserved. And His perfect righteousness—the active obedience of His whole life and the passive obedience of His death—is reckoned, imputed, to us who deserve none, so that we stand before God clothed in a righteousness not our own. He took our place under wrath; we take His place under favor. He was treated as the sinner that we might be treated as the righteous. This is double imputation: our sin to Him, His righteousness to us, neither by infusion nor by our own works, but by the free grace of God laying hold of Christ by faith alone. The dictionary holds the Great Exchange as the very marrow of the gospel and the ground of all assurance: the believer’s sin is fully answered and his righteousness fully supplied, both in Christ, so that there is now no condemnation to them which are in Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The gospel transaction in which the believer’s sin is imputed to Christ, who bore its curse, and Christ’s perfect righteousness is imputed to the believer—double imputation received by faith alone.

expand to see more

THE GREAT EXCHANGE, the double imputation at the heart of justification.

Founded on 2 Corinthians 5:21, “he hath made him to be sin for us.”

Our sin and guilt laid upon Christ, who bore the curse we deserved.

His perfect righteousness imputed to us who deserve none.

Received not by works nor infusion, but by the free grace of God through faith alone.

📖 Key Scripture

2Co 5:21 — "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."

Isa 53:6 — "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all."

Php 3:9 — "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:"

1Pe 2:24 — "Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The exchange is denied or hollowed out by schemes that reject imputed righteousness for infused or self-attained righteousness.

expand to see more

The reigning corruption denies the imputation that makes the exchange possible. The Roman scheme replaces imputed righteousness with infused righteousness—a grace worked within that the sinner must cooperate with and complete—so that justification rests partly on the believer’s own renewed life. Various modern revisions of Paul likewise empty the exchange, denying that Christ’s active obedience is reckoned to us and reducing justification to covenant membership or future vindication by works.

The dictionary holds the double imputation as Scripture states it. He who knew no sin was made sin; we who have no righteousness are made the righteousness of God in Him. The exchange is forensic and complete, received by faith alone apart from works, and it is the only secure ground of a guilty sinner’s peace. To dilute it—making our righteousness partly our own, or Christ’s sin-bearing a mere example—is to rob the soul of the one robe that fits it for the presence of a holy God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase names the mutual transfer of Scripture: our sin to Christ, His righteousness to us, by imputation.

expand to see more

Greek logizomai — to reckon, impute, credit to one’s account; the verb of imputation.

Greek hamartia — sin; “he made him to be sin for us.”

Greek dikaiosunē — righteousness; “the righteousness of God in him.”

Luther’s phrase, the “happy exchange,” admirabile commercium.

The exchange is double: our guilt imputed to Christ, His righteousness imputed to us.

Usage

"The Great Exchange is preached as the marrow of the gospel and the ground of assurance."

"It is summarized from 2 Corinthians 5:21 as the clearest statement of double imputation."

"It is set against schemes of infused or self-attained righteousness."
